title: The Grammarian's Son: Philadelphia, Building 20, and the Two Careers
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: East Oak Lane: The Grammarian's House

stops.name: East Oak Lane, Philadelphia, the birth
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: In a neighborhood of row houses on the northern edge of the city, a son is born to William Chomsky and Elsie Simonofsky, both children of Ashkenazi immigrants out of the Russian empire. The father is a Hebrew grammarian who will spend a career on the medieval philologist David Kimhi; the mother teaches and runs Hebrew classes in the same circles. They name the boy Avram Noam. Hebrew is argued over at the table long before the child can read English with any ease. Grammar in this house is the family trade.
suggested_refs: The East Oak Lane neighborhood of Philadelphia, north of the Logan and Olney districts with which it is often confused

stops.name: Broad and York Streets, the father's school
stops.date_confidence: inferred. William Chomsky taught Hebrew at Gratz College and directed the religious school attached to the Mikveh Israel congregation through the 1930s and 1940s; no single dated occasion anchors the boy's presence, and the year is set here only to place the household. The congregation stood at Broad and York from 1909 to 1976, so the well-circulated coordinate for its Fourth Street synagogue is four decades wrong for this period.
stops.campa: His father teaches at Gratz College and directs the religious school of the Mikveh Israel congregation, then standing at Broad and York on the same campus as Dropsie. The son grows up inside that apparatus: prayer, morphology, and the Zionist argument in its labor and its binationalist versions, all of it conducted as scholarship rather than as piety. That a language has a structure, and that the structure can be written down, is a household premise here before it is anybody's thesis. Elsie runs classes of her own. The politics of the house are left, Jewish, and cultural rather than statist.
suggested_refs: The Mikveh Israel synagogue at Broad and York Streets, 1909-1976, adjacent to Gratz and Dropsie Colleges
sources: Robert Barsky, 'Noam Chomsky: A Life of Dissent'

stops.name: Oak Lane Country Day School, the fall of Barcelona
stops.date_confidence: attested to February 1939 by Chomsky's own repeated accounts; the day is not recorded and is defaulted. Note the contradiction in the assembled record: one lens dates the article 1938, which cannot be right, since Barcelona fell on 26 January 1939. The school itself stood in Cheltenham Township, Montgomery County, not in Philadelphia, and is frequently placed inside the city by biographers.
stops.campa: He is enrolled at two years old in a Deweyite country day school north of the city line, where no student is ranked against another and each is left to follow whatever interests him. What interests him is the news from Europe. At ten he writes for the school paper on the fall of Barcelona and on the spread of fascism across the continent, from Austria through Czechoslovakia to Spain. He will describe it for the rest of his life as the first political writing he ever did, and he is still describing it to interviewers in his nineties. The article itself does not survive.
suggested_refs: Oak Lane Day School, White Road, Cheltenham Township, on its original campus before the 1965 move to Blue Bell

stops.name: Central High School, the Olney campus
stops.date_confidence: attested to the years 1940-1945; the month is the ordinary start of term and the day is defaulted. The commonly cited Broad and Green address belongs to the building Central left in 1939, before he arrived.
stops.campa: He transfers to the selective public academic high school, by then removed to a new campus at Ogontz and Olney Avenues, and finds it the opposite of the school he came from: ranked, graded, competitive, and dull. He does well in it and remembers almost nothing of it afterward. What he remembers of these years happens elsewhere. On trains north out of the city and in secondhand bookshops he is reading the anarchist press and the literature of the Spanish collectives, while at Ogontz and Olney his teachers set exercises.
suggested_refs: Central High School of Philadelphia, 184th class, Ogontz and Olney Avenues

stops.name: Seventy-second Street, the uncle's newsstand
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction as to the exact year. The trips begin around age twelve or thirteen, which places their start in 1941 or 1942; no single visit is dated. Month and day are defaulted.
stops.campa: At the back of a subway exit on the Upper West Side his uncle keeps a newsstand, obtained under a Depression-era disability program, and around it gathers a floating seminar of refugee intellectuals, Freudians, Trotskyists, and anarchists who argue past midnight over the papers on the rack. The nephew, twelve and thirteen years old, takes the train up from Philadelphia to listen. The Fourth Avenue book row is a separate haunt further south, and later accounts routinely merge the two places into one. It is here, at the stand, that he reads Rudolf Rocker.
stops.quote: I used to hang around the stand a lot, and it was a real education.
stops.quote_source: Chomsky, autobiographical remarks in interview (Understanding Power)
suggested_refs: The 72nd Street subway newsstand, Upper West Side, run by Chomsky's uncle under a disability compensation program
sources: Chomsky interviewed by Amy Goodman, chomsky.info/20041126

segments.name: Penn: Zellig Harris and the Kibbutz

stops.name: University of Pennsylvania, the meeting with Zellig Harris
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1945 enrolment; month is the start of term and day defaulted. The meeting with Harris through the Avukah circle is dated to 1947 and is folded into this stop rather than given a pin of its own.
stops.campa: He enrols at sixteen in philosophy, logic, and Arabic, paying part of his way by teaching Hebrew to children on Sunday mornings, and within two years is bored enough to consider leaving the country to work on a binationalist kibbutz. Zellig Harris is a structural linguist and, more to the point for the student, a fixture of Avukah, the radical Zionist student circle. They meet over politics rather than over syntax. Harris then puts him to work on the descriptive analysis of Hebrew, the language of his father's trade and of his own childhood. He does not leave for the kibbutz.
suggested_refs: Avukah, the radical Zionist student organization at Penn, through which Chomsky and Harris first met
sources: New Voices, 'A portrait of Chomsky as a young Zionist'

stops.name: Philadelphia, marriage to Carol Schatz
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1949; the month follows the geography lens and the day is defaulted. The relationship is dated to 1947 in the chronology, though the two have known each other since early childhood.
stops.campa: He marries Carol Doris Schatz, whom he has known since they were small children in the same Hebrew-school circle, she five and he seven. The wedding joins two families out of the same few streets in the north of the city. The marriage will last fifty-nine years and end only with her death. Two years afterward he submits a master's thesis on the morphophonemics of Modern Hebrew, later published as a book: a formal description of the sound system of the language spoken over his parents' table.
suggested_refs: 'Morphophonemics of Modern Hebrew', the 1951 master's thesis, published later as a book

stops.name: Kibbutz HaZore'a, six weeks in the Jezreel Valley
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1953; the stay was six weeks, and accounts giving several months overstate it. Month and day are defaulted. The coordinate falls within about three hundred metres of the kibbutz.
stops.campa: On a Harvard travel grant he and Carol cross England, France, Switzerland, and Italy, and then spend six weeks living and working on a kibbutz of the Hashomer Hatzair movement in the Jezreel Valley. He finds the labor and the common ownership genuinely good, and says later that he came close to returning there to live. He never afterward reports that without the rest of it: an anti-Arab racism he had not expected, and a membership arguing the merits of Stalin.
suggested_refs: Kibbutz HaZore'a, Hashomer Hatzair, in the Jezreel Valley
sources: 'Look Back to Galilee: Chomsky and the Kibbutz'

stops.name: University of Pennsylvania, the doctorate
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1955; month and day defaulted to the ordinary degree calendar.
stops.campa: The doctorate is awarded for a dissertation on transformational analysis cut out of the far larger manuscript he has been writing at Harvard, which no publisher will take and which circulates for two decades in microfilm before anyone prints it. What he is arguing his way out of, respectfully and page by page, is Harris's own procedure for discovering a grammar in a body of recorded speech. The committee sits at Penn. In any working sense the thing is unsupervised.
suggested_refs: 'Transformational Analysis', the 1955 Penn dissertation, chapter of the unpublished 'Logical Structure of Linguistic Theory'

segments.name: Cambridge: The Society of Fellows and Building 20

stops.name: Harvard Yard, the Society of Fellows
stops.date_confidence: attested to the years 1951-1955; month and day are defaulted to the start of the fellowship year. The pin is the corpus's canonical Harvard Yard coordinate.
stops.campa: Elected a Junior Fellow at twenty-two, he is given four years, a stipend, and no obligation whatever to produce anything. He spends them on the manuscript that becomes The Logical Structure of Linguistic Theory: close to a thousand pages arguing that the sentences of a language are generated by a finite system of rules and that the proper object of linguistics is that system rather than the corpus of things people happen to have said. Around him at Harvard are Nelson Goodman and Willard Van Orman Quine, whose empiricism the manuscript is dismantling page by page. He shows it to almost no one.
suggested_refs: 'The Logical Structure of Linguistic Theory', written 1955-1956, circulated in microfilm, published 1975

stops.name: Harvard Yard, J. L. Austin comes over from Oxford
stops.date_confidence: attested in j_l_austin.journey.json to April 1955; the day is not fixed there and is defaulted here. The stop is held at the corpus's canonical Harvard Yard pin, inherited byte for byte.
stops.campa: J. L. Austin arrives from Oxford to lecture on the utterances that describe nothing and instead perform an act, and the two men meet. Austin asks what a sentence does between people, and answers with promises, verdicts, and the conditions under which they misfire. Chomsky, twenty-six, asks what a sentence is inside a head, and answers that it is the output of a rule system no speaker can state. Neither account closes the other, and neither man converts. Austin will be dead within five years. The lectures he is giving that spring become How to Do Things with Words.
suggested_refs: Austin's William James Lectures at Harvard, 1955, published as 'How to Do Things with Words'

stops.name: MIT, Building 20
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1955; month and day defaulted. Roman Jakobson's role in securing the appointment is attested.
stops.campa: He joins the Research Laboratory of Electronics on Roman Jakobson's word and takes a room in the plywood building the Navy threw up in 1943 as temporary radar space, which the Institute has never got round to demolishing. The corridors hold an acoustics laboratory, a machine shop, a nuclear science group, and the model railroad club whose members are inventing a vocabulary for computers. Morris Halle takes the adjoining office. The heating is poor, and a wall can be cut through with a saw when a project needs more room.
suggested_refs: Building 20, MIT, the wartime radar structure that housed the Research Laboratory of Electronics

stops.name: MIT, Syntactic Structures
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1957; month and day defaulted. The pin is the corpus's canonical MIT coordinate, inherited byte for byte. His daughter Aviva is born the same year, the place recorded in the sources only as Massachusetts.
stops.campa: A monograph cut down out of his course notes argues that a language is an infinite set of sentences generated by finite means, that statistical models of word sequences cannot produce it, and that a grammar is a formal object to be evaluated the way any other theory is evaluated. Within a decade the field has reorganized itself around the book, and the reorganization takes the form of a generation of students arriving in Cambridge to work on rules. His daughter Aviva is born the same year. The sources record the place only as Massachusetts.
suggested_refs: 'Syntactic Structures' (1957), the founding text of generative grammar

stops.name: MIT, Cartesian Linguistics
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1966; month and day defaulted. The 1961 full professorship and the founding of the doctoral program are attested and folded into this stop.
stops.campa: Made full professor in 1961 and by now running a doctoral program that is turning the Institute into the world center of his field, he publishes a short book claiming an ancestry. Rene Descartes and the Port-Royal grammarians held that the mind comes furnished with what experience does not supply, and that the endless novelty of ordinary speech is the proof that no machine is doing it. The innate language faculty, he says, is that same claim in modern dress, and he wants the seventeenth century entered as evidence. Historians of philosophy object to the reading. He does not much retreat from it.
suggested_refs: 'Cartesian Linguistics: A Chapter in the History of Rationalist Thought' (1966)
rene_descartes.journey.json, for the rationalist theory of innate ideas Chomsky claims as ancestor
sources: MIT News on the founding of the linguistics doctoral program

stops.name: Boston, the church basements
stops.date_confidence: 1962 is Chomsky's own dating of the start of his public protest against the war; the individual meetings are not itemized in any reachable source, and month and day are defaulted. The pin is Boston generally, not a particular hall.
stops.campa: He begins speaking against the war in churches, living rooms, and small halls around Boston. He is by this point a tenured professor at an institute funded substantially by the Defense Department, arguing in public that the war it serves is a crime, and he expects the career to end over it. The career does not end, and the speaking does not stop; it will keep him on the road for most of the next decade. At these first meetings the audience is sometimes four people, and sometimes only the organizers who arranged the hall.
suggested_refs: The Boston-area antiwar meeting circuit of 1962-1965, before the movement had numbers

stops.name: Cambridge, The Responsibility of Intellectuals
stops.date_confidence: attested to February 1967. The essay is published in The New York Review of Books in New York; the pin is where it was written and where its author taught, since the writing rather than the printing is his own act.
stops.campa: The New York Review of Books prints his essay on the men who supply the reasons of state: that it is the responsibility of intellectuals to speak the truth and to expose lies, that they have the training and the leisure and the access to do it, and that the ones staffing this war have instead made themselves its technicians. The essay travels further than any linguistics he has written, and it is reprinted and translated for decades afterward. He names the men. He quotes their own published sentences back at them.
suggested_refs: 'The Responsibility of Intellectuals', The New York Review of Books, 23 February 1967

stops.name: Boston Common, the start of Stop the Draft Week
stops.date_confidence: attested. A photograph in the UMass Amherst collections is captioned 'Noam Chomsky speaking at rally on Boston Common, October 16, 1967'. Note the frequent conflation: the draft-card burning that day was at Arlington Street Church, later, and is given its own stop.
stops.campa: He speaks on the Common at the opening of Stop the Draft Week, one of a group that has founded RESIST earlier in the year with Mitchell Goodman, Denise Levertov, William Sloane Coffin, and Dwight Macdonald, and that has circulated a call to resist illegitimate authority which is itself, under federal law, a conspiracy. Organizers of the week will be indicted for exactly that. The photograph that survives shows him at the microphone in jacket and tie, the bare trees of the Common behind him.
suggested_refs: UMass Amherst, Special Collections, muph009-v04a-sl073-i022, 'Noam Chomsky speaking at rally on Boston Common, October 16, 1967'
sources: Boundary Stones on the 1967 antiwar movement

stops.name: Arlington Street Church, the draft cards
stops.date_confidence: attested. The mass turn-in and burning took place at this Unitarian church on the afternoon of 16 October 1967; the coordinate is the church. Sources that place Chomsky's own speech here have merged it with the Boston Common rally earlier the same day.
stops.campa: Later the same day the crowd moves indoors to a Unitarian church on the Back Bay, where a service is held and young men come forward to burn their draft cards in a candle flame at the altar or hand them up in a collection basket. The design is deliberate and it is not evasion: the act is a crime, committed in a sanctuary, in front of press and clergy and parents, by people who intend the government to know their names. It is the largest such action of the war to that point.
suggested_refs: The Arlington Street Church draft-card service, 16 October 1967, organized by the Resistance
sources: Boundary Stones on the 1967 antiwar movement
Chomsky, 'American Power and the New Mandarins'

stops.name: The Pentagon, the march and the night in custody
stops.date_confidence: attested. The overnight custody at the Occoquan workhouse in Lorton, Virginia is confirmed by Mailer's own account; the workhouse was a District of Columbia institution and not, as often stated, a federal prison.
stops.campa: Five days later he crosses the Potomac with tens of thousands of demonstrators, goes on talking to the crowd as troops in gas masks advance, and is carried off and arrested. The night is spent in the District's workhouse at Lorton, in a cell shared with Norman Mailer, who is at that moment gathering the material for a book and who will put the professor into it. They are released the following day, and he goes back to Cambridge to a term already under way.
suggested_refs: Norman Mailer, 'The Armies of the Night' (1968), which records the shared cell
The Occoquan Workhouse, Lorton, Virginia, a District of Columbia institution
sources: chomsky.info, 'Mayday: The Case for Civil Disobedience'

segments.name: Laos, Hanoi, and the Enemies List

stops.name: Vientiane, the day that became a week
stops.date_confidence: attested to late March 1970; the day is not fixed and is defaulted. He expected to stay one day, missed the International Control Commission flight to Hanoi, and stayed about a week. The refugee camp he visited lay some thirty-five miles out of the city and is folded into this stop rather than given an invented coordinate.
stops.campa: He flies in expecting a single day before the Control Commission plane carries him to Hanoi, misses it, and stays a week in a capital where the American war next door is officially not happening. He interviews Lao officials, Pathet Lao representatives, and refugees at a camp thirty-five miles out of town, peasants cleared off the Plain of Jars whose villages were bombed for years by aircraft no government would admit to sending. He writes it up for the New York Review as a visit to a country nobody is covering.
stops.quote: the interviews... left a permanent mark on my understanding of the war
stops.quote_source: Chomsky, 'A Visit to Laos', The New York Review of Books, 23 July 1970
suggested_refs: Chomsky, 'A Visit to Laos', NYRB, 23 July 1970
The Plain of Jars evacuation and the American bombing of northern Laos

stops.name: Hanoi, a week under the bombing pause
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: He reaches Hanoi in April for a week, lectures at the university, and is shown bomb damage in the city and in the countryside around it. The account he publishes afterward is careful, and careful in a way that will be used against him for fifty years: he reports what he is shown, states what he cannot verify, and declines both of the available scripts, the one in which the North is a totalitarian machine and the one in which it is a peasant utopia. Back in Washington an aide is meanwhile compiling a list of names.
suggested_refs: Chomsky, 'In North Vietnam', The New York Review of Books, 13 August 1970

stops.name: The White House, the enemies list
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1971; month and day defaulted. The pin is the White House as the seat of the administration that compiled the list, not a place Chomsky visited that year.
stops.campa: A staff memorandum listing the administration's political opponents, drawn up so that the machinery of federal government can be turned against them, carries the name of a professor of linguistics at MIT. In the same period the Guggenheim Foundation gives him a fellowship, and the National Academy of Sciences elects him a member. He is at once an enemy of the state and an ornament of its scientific establishment. The list itself stays secret until the Watergate hearings, when the names are read into the record of a Senate committee.
suggested_refs: The Nixon administration's list of political opponents, made public during the Watergate hearings

stops.name: Eindhoven, the debate with Michel Foucault
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction as far as this file's verified pool goes. The televised debate on human nature, recorded for Dutch television in 1971, is a well-known and filmed event but is absent from the chronology assembled for this file and from michel_foucault.journey.json, which covers Foucault's Paris prison-group work in the same year and is silent on the broadcast. Month and day are defaulted.
stops.campa: Dutch television seats him opposite Michel Foucault before an audience of students and asks whether there is such a thing as human nature. He says yes: the mind arrives with a fixed structure, and it is that structure which makes a just society thinkable and specifiable in advance of having one. Foucault answers that the notion of justice is itself produced by the system it is being used to judge. The recording survives and the transcript stays in print. They agree about the police, and about very little else.
suggested_refs: The Chomsky-Foucault debate on human nature, De Nederlandse Televisie Stichting, 1971
michel_foucault.journey.json, which does not carry this event
sources: Widely circulated broadcast recording and published transcript; not present in the verified chronology assembled for this file

segments.name: The Libertarian Left and the Propaganda Model

stops.name: London, the Peter Jay interview
stops.date_confidence: attested to 25 July 1976. The pin is London generally; the studio is not named in the reachable transcripts.
stops.campa: Asked on British television to say plainly what his politics are, he does: the libertarian left, anarcho-syndicalism, the enterprises owned and run by the people who work in them, and the state dismantled only as fast as the private tyrannies it currently restrains can be dismantled with it. Mikhail Bakunin had forecast that a revolution which builds a state to win a war ends by losing the revolution, and Chomsky calls that one of the few predictions in the social sciences ever to come true. The lineage he gives is not academic. It runs to Rudolf Rocker, read at thirteen at his uncle's newsstand, and to the Spanish collectives of 1936.
stops.quote: I would prefer to think of it as the libertarian left, and from that point of view anarchism can be conceived as a kind of voluntary socialism, that is, as libertarian socialist or anarcho-syndicalist or communist anarchist.
stops.quote_source: 'The Relevance of Anarcho-Syndicalism', Noam Chomsky interviewed by Peter Jay, 25 July 1976, transcript at chomsky.info/19760725
suggested_refs: Chomsky's 1970 introduction to Rudolf Rocker's 'Anarcho-Syndicalism'
mikhail_bakunin.journey.json, for the forecast about the revolutionary state and the Barcelona collectives of 1936-1937

stops.name: MIT, Institute Professor
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1976; month and day defaulted. He had held the Ferrari P. Ward Professorship from 1966. Accounts that stage the appointment at commencement in Killian Court have invented a ceremony: Institute Professor is an internal faculty appointment.
stops.campa: MIT makes him Institute Professor, its highest faculty rank, ten years after giving him a named chair. He is by now the most publicly denounced man on the faculty, and the department he built is the world center of his field; the Institute has decided, without ever saying so, that it will carry both. There is no ceremony. The appointment is an act of the faculty and a line in a memorandum. His office hours do not change, and he goes on answering letters from strangers.
suggested_refs: The Institute Professorship, MIT's highest faculty appointment, held by Chomsky from 1976

stops.name: Paris, the Faurisson preface
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1980; month and day defaulted. The pin is Paris as the center of the French press controversy, not a place Chomsky travelled to over the affair.
stops.campa: He signs a petition defending the right of Robert Faurisson, a French literature lecturer who denies the Nazi extermination of the Jews, to publish without interference from the state or from mobs, and writes a short essay on freedom of expression which he says may be used as the recipients see fit. It appears as the preface to Faurisson's book, without his knowledge. He states that he regards Faurisson's claims as false and repellent and that a right to speak is not an endorsement of what is said. In France the distinction is not accepted. His standing there never recovers.
suggested_refs: 'Some Elementary Comments on the Rights of Freedom of Expression' (1980), printed as the preface without Chomsky's knowledge

stops.name: Universidad Centroamericana, the Managua lectures
stops.date_confidence: attested to March 1986; the day is not fixed and is defaulted. Flagged contradiction in the assembled record: one lens dates the visit 1985, the other 1986. The publishers of both lecture volumes date the series to March 1986, and this file follows them without pretending the discrepancy did not exist.
stops.campa: He gives five lectures at the Jesuit university in Managua at the height of the contra war, in a country under embargo with its harbors mined, and he does not spend them telling the audience that its revolution is admirable. He tells them what the United States is, how its press works, and why the destruction of Nicaragua is a rational policy from the standpoint of the interests that decide such things. He gives a second series on the same visit, on language and the problems of knowledge: syntax in the morning, empire in the evening. Both series are published as books.
suggested_refs: 'On Power and Ideology: The Managua Lectures' (1987)
'Language and Problems of Knowledge: The Managua Lectures' (1988)
sources: South End Press and MIT Press notes to the two Managua volumes

stops.name: MIT, the propaganda model
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1988; month and day defaulted. The pin is Chomsky's own workplace; his co-author Edward Herman worked at the Wharton School in Philadelphia, and the book has no single site.
stops.campa: With Edward Herman, whose collaboration with him goes back to the Vietnam-era propaganda studies of 1973, he sets out a model rather than a complaint. News passes through filters, of ownership, advertising, sourcing, organized flak, and a designated enemy, so that a press with no censor and no orders reliably produces what a censored press would produce. It becomes the most widely read thing either man ever writes. The test cases are set side by side: two mass killings of comparable scale, one of them covered and one of them not.
suggested_refs: 'Manufacturing Consent: The Political Economy of the Mass Media' (1988)
Mark Achbar and Peter Wintonick, 'Manufacturing Consent: Noam Chomsky and the Media' (1992), the documentary built on the book, centered on New York Times coverage of East Timor

stops.name: Kyoto, the prize in basic sciences
stops.date_confidence: attested to 11 November 1988, the date of the commemorative lectures at the Kyoto International Conference Center, with a follow-on workshop the next day.
stops.campa: The Inamori Foundation gives him its prize in basic sciences for the theory of generative grammar, one of the three it awards in Kyoto each November, and he flies to Japan to deliver the commemorative lecture, on language and mind, their challenges and their prospects. He speaks at the International Conference Center; a workshop follows the next day. The citation is for the linguistics alone, and nothing said in the hall over the two days refers to the other library he has written, the one on American foreign policy.
suggested_refs: The 1988 Kyoto Prize commemorative lecture, 'Language and Mind: Challenges and Prospects'
sources: kyotoprize.org, laureate page and 1988 speech archive

stops.name: Sydney Town Hall, East Timor
stops.date_confidence: attested to January 1995; the day is not recorded in the reachable account and is defaulted.
stops.campa: He fills the town hall twenty years after Indonesia's invasion of East Timor and tells an Australian audience what its own government did: recognized the annexation, did business with the occupier, and helped train its officers. The Australian press, which did not cover the occupation, covers the lecture, and reports the size of the crowd. He has been writing about the territory since the killing began in 1975, through years when almost no editor in the English-speaking world would print the figures.
suggested_refs: The 1995 Australian speaking tour and the twentieth anniversary of the invasion of East Timor
sources: Contemporary accounts of the 1995 Australian visit

stops.name: Universidad de Buenos Aires, the honorary doctorate
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The degree is recorded without a year in the reachable sources; the date here carries no evidential weight and exists only to order the segment. The relation itself is attested.
stops.campa: The university confers a doctorate honoris causa. No source that can be reached gives the year, and the missing date is itself a fact about the relation. He writes about the region as an object of United States policy, and the region reads him as a witness for the prosecution. In Latin America he is less an honored foreign visitor than a standing citation: read aloud in student assemblies, quoted in pamphlets, translated by people who will never meet him.
suggested_refs: Wikidata, honorary doctorate of the University of Buenos Aires
The Spanish-language translation and circulation of Chomsky's political writing in the Southern Cone
sources: Wikipedia, 'List of honorary degrees awarded to Noam Chomsky'

stops.name: University of Delhi, the Delhi lectures
stops.date_confidence: attested for a 2001 visit; month and day defaulted. Flagged: the volume 'Democracy and Power: The Delhi Lectures' collects talks from two visits, 1996 and 2001, and does not record a single 2001 series as one lens implies.
stops.campa: He lectures in Delhi on democracy, corporate power, and the order that emerged after 1989, to audiences of a size no American university offers him. He is received in India as a public figure rather than as a professor, which is the pattern everywhere outside the United States and has been for thirty years. The economist Jean Dreze will later gather these talks together with those of a visit five years earlier into a single volume, so that two trips appear in print as one occasion.
suggested_refs: 'Democracy and Power: The Delhi Lectures', ed. Jean Dreze, Open Book Publishers, 2014
sources: Open Book Publishers, 'Introduction: Chomsky in India'
Wikipedia, 'List of honorary degrees awarded to Noam Chomsky'

stops.name: Cambridge, the September and the last teaching year
stops.date_confidence: attested to September 2001; the date given is the day of the attacks, and the interviews run through the weeks after it. The 2002 retirement is attested and folded into this stop.
stops.campa: In the days after the attacks the telephone does not stop. He gives interviews to whoever asks, in a dozen countries, and repeats one argument: that the atrocity was a crime, that crimes are answered by law and not by bombardment, and that the United States has done to others what has now been done to it. The transcripts are collected into a thin book that sells in the hundreds of thousands. The following year he retires from the faculty, forty-seven years after Jakobson brought him in.
suggested_refs: MIT News, 'Chomsky Is Citation Champ' (1992), on the Arts and Humanities Citation Index count
The MIT Libraries deed of the Noam Chomsky Papers, over 260 boxes, 2012
sources: MIT ArchivesSpace, Noam Chomsky personal archives

stops.name: Istanbul State Security Court, the co-defendant
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The publisher Fatih Tas is on trial for treason for printing an essay of Chomsky's on the Turkish state's war against the Kurds, and Chomsky flies to Istanbul and asks the court to try him as co-defendant, on the ground that he wrote the thing. The court now has the author in the room demanding prosecution and an international press bench watching it decide. The prosecutor asks for acquittal on the first day. Tas is acquitted. The trial has lasted an afternoon.
suggested_refs: Human Rights Watch, 'Turkey: Acquittal in Chomsky Case Is Step in Right Direction', 14 February 2002

stops.name: Porto Alegre, the World Social Forum
stops.date_confidence: attested to late January 2003, the closing session; the day is defaulted. Flagged: the interlock lens carried this as reconstruction, and it is not. Democracy Now! and contemporary reports place him on the platform in a football stadium.
stops.campa: He speaks at the closing session in a football stadium, before something like fifteen thousand people, sharing the platform with Arundhati Roy, six weeks before the invasion of Iraq. The announced subject is a world without wars. The movement in front of him is the one the press has agreed to call anti-globalization, and he tells it that it is the only genuinely international movement now in existence, and that the accurate word for the thing it opposes is not globalization but investor rights.
suggested_refs: Democracy Now!, 18 February 2003, 'Noam Chomsky Speaks at the World Social Forum in Brazil'
Hugo Chavez holding up 'Hegemony or Survival' at the United Nations rostrum, 20 September 2006, recorded in hugo_chavez.journey.json
sources: Contemporary reports of the third World Social Forum

stops.name: American University of Beirut, the first Lebanese visit
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: He and Carol arrive in Lebanon for the first time and he lectures on power at the university's American Studies center on two consecutive days, in a city rebuilt out of a fifteen-year civil war and still living with the consequences of the last invasion at its southern edge. The audience is Lebanese, Palestinian, and American. He is seventy-seven and keeps the touring schedule of a much younger man. Two months later Israeli aircraft will be over these same neighborhoods.
suggested_refs: Assaf Kfoury, 'Noam Chomsky in Beirut', ZNetwork, 2006

stops.name: The southern suburbs of Beirut, meeting Hassan Nasrallah
stops.date_confidence: attested to May 2006; the day is not fixed in the reachable press and is defaulted. The coordinate for the residence area in the southern suburbs is approximate.
stops.campa: On the same visit he is driven into the southern suburbs to meet the secretary-general of Hezbollah, and says afterward that the organization's weapons are a response to an occupation, and that the disarmament being demanded of it is demanded of nobody else in the region. The regional press carries the meeting within the week. In the United States it circulates for a decade afterward in the form of a photograph with no argument attached to it. He neither withdraws the position nor makes the visit again.
suggested_refs: Regional press coverage of the May 2006 Beirut visit, two months before the July war
sources: MEMRI and ZNetwork coverage of the May 2006 visit

stops.name: The Allenby Bridge, entry denied
stops.date_confidence: attested. He described about five hours at the crossing with roughly two hours of intermittent questioning; the widely repeated 'three hours of questioning' is a compression of that.
stops.campa: Israeli border guards hold him about five hours at the crossing from Jordan, question him on and off for two of them, ask what he thinks of the Israeli government and whether he has ever lectured at an Israeli university, and then stamp the passport: two red lines, the words Entry denied in Hebrew and in an English that misspells the word entry. He is eighty-one years old. The interior ministry calls it a misunderstanding by an official at the bridge. The officials at the bridge say they were following instructions.
suggested_refs: Democracy Now!, 17 May 2010, 'Denied Entry: Israel Blocks Noam Chomsky from Entering West Bank', full transcript

stops.name: Amman, the lecture by video link
stops.date_confidence: attested to 18 May 2010, two days after the refusal, delivered from the University of Jordan. Flagged: one lens dated the link to the same day as the border refusal and placed it in a hotel; the Democracy Now! transcript of 17 May has him describing it as still to come.
stops.campa: Two days after the refusal he gives the lecture anyway, by video link from a hall at the University of Jordan, to about a hundred students gathered on the Birzeit campus some twenty miles away on the far side of a river he is not permitted to cross. Interviewed the day before, he had described the arrangement as still to be settled. The announced subject was the Palestinian question. He says at the start that the arrangement makes the argument more economically than the lecture will. Then he delivers the lecture as written.
suggested_refs: The students assembled at Birzeit University, north of Ramallah, to watch the link on 18 May 2010
sources: Al Jazeera coverage of the incident

stops.name: Dewey Square, Occupy Boston
stops.date_confidence: attested to 2011; the day of his appearance is not fixed in the reachable sources and is defaulted to the month of the encampment.
stops.campa: He comes down to the tents and tells the encampment that what it is protesting is not a scandal but a design: thirty years of policy moving wealth upward, and a financial sector that owns the process by which it is regulated. He is eighty-two. He has been making this argument since before most of the people in front of him were born, and says as much, without any particular emphasis. The occupation is a few weeks old. Police will clear it in December.
suggested_refs: The Occupy Boston encampment at Dewey Square, September to December 2011

stops.name: Sao Paulo, the second marriage
stops.date_confidence: attested to 2014; month and day are not recorded in the reachable sources and are defaulted. The couple hold a residence in the city from 2015.
stops.campa: Carol died in 2008, at seventy-eight, after fifty-nine years of marriage. Six years later he marries Valeria Wasserman, a Brazilian translator who has worked on his books into Portuguese. He is eighty-five at the wedding. From the following year the couple keep a residence in her city, and the shape of his old age is set: an American academic base and a Brazilian home. He works from whichever of the two he is in, and the interviews go on at the same rate as before.
suggested_refs: Carol Chomsky's obituary, Philadelphia Inquirer, December 2008

stops.name: MIT, the founding collective of DiEM25
stops.date_confidence: attested for the membership and the launch date; the pin is deliberately Chomsky's own base and not Berlin, because he was not in the room. The Volksbuhne launch on Rosa-Luxemburg-Platz belongs to yanis_varoufakis.journey.json, which carries it.
stops.campa: His name appears on the first coordinating collective of a movement launched from a theatre on Rosa-Luxemburg-Platz by Yanis Varoufakis, four months out of the Greek finance ministry, alongside Brian Eno, Elif Shafak, and Vivienne Westwood. What he lends is a name that certifies a project as serious to a particular constituency, and the argument that the European institutions are unaccountable in exactly the way private power has always been unaccountable. He is eighty-seven. He is not in Berlin.
suggested_refs: yanis_varoufakis.journey.json, for the Volksbuhne launch of DiEM25, 9 February 2016

stops.name: University of Arizona, the desert chair
stops.date_confidence: attested. The appointment was announced on 17 August by the College of Social and Behavioral Sciences for the fall term.
stops.campa: At eighty-eight he takes a chair at Arizona as laureate professor of linguistics, holding the Agnese Nelms Haury chair in the College of Social and Behavioral Sciences, and moves his base from Massachusetts to the Sonoran desert after sixty-two years in Cambridge. The college announces it in August, for the fall term. He keeps a full schedule of public talks, and the interviews continue at a rate of several a week, conducted now from Tucson rather than from Cambridge. He teaches. The seminars fill.
suggested_refs: University of Arizona, College of Social and Behavioral Sciences, 'The Home of Noam Chomsky'

stops.name: Tucson, the stroke
stops.date_confidence: attested to June 2023; the day is not public and is defaulted. Flagged: one lens placed the stroke in Sao Paulo. It happened in the United States, where he was based, and the flight to Brazil came afterward.
stops.campa: In June he suffers a massive stroke. It takes his speech and the use of his right side, and the man who has spent sixty-eight years explaining what a sentence is cannot produce one. He goes on unpaid medical leave from the university that October. Reporting out of Brazil, from his family, describes him following conversation and reading, and answering with his left hand. Valeria arranges an air ambulance and waits for him to be stable enough to fly.
suggested_refs: Folha de S.Paulo reporting on his condition, relayed by AP and NBC News, June 2024
sources: Tucson.com, 'Noam Chomsky hospitalized after massive stroke'

stops.name: Sao Paulo, the hospital
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction as to the month. The transfer is attested; the flight took place once he was stable, some weeks after the June stroke, and the exact date is not public. Day defaulted.
stops.campa: He is flown south with two nurses aboard and admitted to a hospital near his wife's family, where a neurologist, a speech therapist, and a lung specialist see him daily. Four thousand miles north, the MIT Libraries hold more than two hundred and sixty boxes of his papers and are putting them online, and the citation indexes still record him as the most cited living person. Valeria tells reporters that he follows the news, that he reads, and that he answers with his left hand.
suggested_refs: MIT Libraries, the Noam Chomsky papers, 1945-2013, deeded 2012 and digitized from 2017
sources: MIT ArchivesSpace, Noam Chomsky personal archives
